    Statement
    United States of America
    His Excellency
    Donald Trump
    President
    22 September 2026
    Kaltura

    Daily summary

    Meetings Coverage - Live

    ‘I acted, while others talked,’ says United States President

    “While others have talked, I have acted; while others have spoken of peace, I have made peace,” said United States President Donald J. Trump, turning to “the number one sponsor of terror”, Iran.  

    For 51 years, the fanatical Iranian regime has ruled by bloodshed and mass murder, spreading death, carnage and chaos across the entire Middle East and beyond.  

    Never allow Iran to have nuclear weapons

    “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he insisted, recalling that he offered Tehran full economic cooperation for ending their nuclear programme and support for terror.  However, they refused.

    Through Operation Midnight Hammer, the US military obliterated their nuclear programme beneath mountains of rubble.   As a result of Operation Epic Fury, all 159 ships of their navy are lying at the bottom of the sea.  

    “I have a big decision to make – will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before […] or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again,” he said, adding:  “I believe we make a deal right after the elections”.

    Trump on Ukraine:  ‘We will get that one done’

    “Since I took office, it has been my great honour to settle eight wars, many of which had gone on for years or even decades,” he continued.

    In Gaza, he said, the United States has ended the war, “saving untold thousands of lives” and brought home all remaining hostages, both living and dead.

    On Ukraine, Washington, D.C., was working very closely with the leaders of the Russian Federation and Ukraine.

    “We will get that one done,” he said, adding:  “It is going to happen quicker than people understand.”  Some 25,000 young people — mostly soldiers — are dying each month, he said, pointing to “horrible battlefield pictures”.

    Turning to Venezuela and the arrest of its “outlaw dictator”, Nicolás Maduro, he said hundreds of Venezuelan political prisoners had since been freed.  Last month, the United States signed what he described as “the largest oil deal in history”, which will benefit both countries.

    Washington’s actions in Venezuela demonstrate that the United States “will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere”, he said, adding that, if necessary, his country would use its “unmatched military might” to secure its vital national interests.

    Trump turns on Mexico

    On his Administration’s fight against drug cartels — which he described as “the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere” — he said their members should be “killed, exiled or detained”.  To that end, the United States has carried out a dozen strikes, including the termination of the leader of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua.  He described Mexico as “the epicentre of cartel violence”. 

    Trump on Greenland, sweeping UN reform

    In Greenland, the United States will “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence” in appropriate locations, including the construction of “two very major military bases”.

    The agreement with Denmark and Greenland will be signed later today, he added.

    Furthermore, his Administration has worked with many countries to implement “the most sweeping reform in UN history”.

    The Organization’s budget was cut for the first time, he said, by 15 per cent in 2026, while over 4,000 positions were eliminated from its bureaucracy.  

    UN urged to stop imposing globalist agenda

    While the United Nations has “great potential”, it must “stop imposing the far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected”, he said.

    “There is no global government, and while I am President, there will be no global taxes,” he stressed.  He also called on all States Parties to the International Criminal Court to formally withdraw from this “rogue institution”.

    Calling Iran “the number one sponsor of terror,” the President devoted much of his speech to the Islamic Republic, arguing that his Administration had confronted a threat that previous leaders – in the US and abroad – had failed to address.

    He told world leaders gathered in the Assembly Hall for the annual General Debate that for 51 years, “the fanatical Iranian regime” had spread “carnage and chaos” across the entire Middle East and beyond.

    Nuclear weapons ban 
    “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

    Mr. Trump said his administration had offered Iran economic cooperation in exchange for ending its nuclear programme and support for terrorism, but that Tehran had rejected the proposal.

    “Then in Operation Midnight Hammer, the US military obliterated their nuclear programme beneath mountains of rubble,” he said.

    The President went on to claim that subsequent military operations had severely weakened Iran’s military capabilities, citing the destruction of naval assets, air defences and missile production facilities.

    “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked.

    But he also described a binary choice, over whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” and “drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness.”

    Mr. Trump predicted an agreement would eventually be reached. “I believe we’ll make a deal," he said.

    Calling for continued international unity, he urged countries to support the “complete economic isolation of Iran” until it ended attacks on commercial shipping and support for terrorism.

    Wars settled, conflicts addressed
    Turning to broader foreign policy, Mr. Trump said he had helped bring an end to eight conflicts since returning to office.

    Among those he listed were disputes involving Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as the war in Gaza.

    The President also said efforts were continuing to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

    “It's time to stop the killing,” he said.

    Pressure in the Americas
    Mr. Trump highlighted a series of developments across the Western Hemisphere, including what he described as a US military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the arrest of President Nicolás Maduro.

    He said the US was now working with Venezuelan leaders toward what he called “a much better future for the Venezuelan people” and announced a major oil agreement between the two countries.

    On Mexico, the President focused on efforts against transnational crime, saying drug cartels had been designated as foreign terrorist organizations and calling on the country to “reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity.”

    He also cited ongoing negotiations with Cuba, saying his administration sought "a fundamental change in the situation” there.

    The President also lauded the new agreement due to be signed with Greenland, describing the Arctic territory as strategically important to regional and international security.

    Mr. Trump said the arrangement with Denmark and Greenland would give the United States "permanent control over security and all other needs" on the territory and would support NATO's security posture in the Arctic and North Atlantic regions.

    From AI to ‘superintelligence’
    A significant portion of the address also focused on artificial intelligence (AI), which Mr. Trump argued should instead be called “superintelligence.”

    “The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake,” he said. “It is not fake. It's actually amazing.”

    President Trump said technological leadership would be central to economic and geopolitical competition in the years ahead.

    “Whoever wins superintelligence wins,” he declared, adding that the US would encourage development of the technology while monitoring potential risks.

    ‘Evil people’
    Mr. Trump also renewed criticism of several international bodies.

    He described the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution “full of evil people” with no jurisdiction over the United States and called on nations to withdraw from it.

    The President was similarly critical of the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Council, accusing it of focusing excessively on the US while overlooking abuses elsewhere.

    He criticized the education, culture and science agency, UNESCO and the International Maritime Organization, arguing that international bodies should not advance what he characterized as global governance initiatives.

    Concluding his address, Mr. Trump called on countries to confront global challenges with “courage and resolve,” saying cooperation among nations could create “a future for our people that is brighter, more hopeful, and more magnificent than ever before.”
